comparisons.peer_summary: Investment banking fees increased $1.5 billion primarily due to higher debt and equity issuance fees and higher advisory fees.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Bank of America attribute increases in investment banking revenues to higher debt and equity issuance fees, alongside stronger advisory activity. Citi reports a specific 38% total increase in Investment Banking revenues, with DCM underwriting fees rising 61% and equity fees rising 38% due to record issuance and follow-on activity. Bank of America reports a broader $1.5 billion increase in investment banking fees, explicitly citing higher debt and equity issuance fees and advisory fees as the primary drivers, mirroring Citi's product-level growth factors.

comparisons.peer_summary: Investment banking revenues were $7.74 billion in 2024, up 24% from 2023, primarily due to significantly higher revenues in debt underwriting (leveraged finance) and equity underwriting (secondary and IPOs), as well as higher advisory revenues from increased M&A activity.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Goldman Sachs report significant year-over-year growth in investment banking revenues driven by strong debt and equity underwriting markets. Citi's Investment Banking revenue grew 38%, fueled by a 61% surge in DCM underwriting fees from near-record debt issuance and a 38% rise in equity underwriting fees. Similarly, Goldman Sachs reported a 24% increase in investment banking revenues to $7.74 billion, primarily reflecting significantly higher revenues in debt underwriting (leveraged finance) and equity underwriting (secondary and IPOs). Both disclosures highlight robust debt issuance activity as a key growth engine.

comparisons.peer_summary: Investment banking fees increased in 2024 due to favorable market conditions, resulting in higher debt underwriting fees from increased leveraged loans and bond issuances, higher equity underwriting fees from IPO and follow-on offerings, and higher advisory fees from increased M&A activity.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and JPMorgan report substantial growth in investment banking fees driven by favorable market conditions and increases across debt, equity, and advisory products. Citi's Investment Banking revenues increased 38%, with DCM fees up 61% and equity fees up 38%, while advisory fees rose 22% due to closing transactions. JPMorgan's investment banking fees also increased, driven by higher industry-wide issuances in leveraged loans and bonds (debt), increased IPO and follow-on fees (equity), and higher M&A activity (advisory). Both firms cite wallet share gains and industry-wide volume increases as contributors to this growth.

sentences.text: Investment Banking revenues increased 38%, reflecting a 42% increase in investment banking fees, due to a rebound in overall wallet activity and wallet share gains across all products.
DCM underwriting fees increased 61%, benefiting from near record debt issuance, particularly in investment grade and higher leveraged finance activity.
Advisory fees increased 22%, due to strong announced deal volume from earlier in the year coming to fruition as those transactions closed.
Equity underwriting fees increased 38%, due to stronger follow-on and convertibles activity.
Investment banking fees increased, reflecting in CIB the benefit of favorable market conditions, which resulted in:
• higher debt underwriting fees predominantly driven by higher industry-wide issuances in leveraged loans, and in high-grade and high-yield bonds,
• higher equity underwriting fees driven by higher industry-wide fees and wallet share gains in IPOs, and in follow-on and convertible securities offerings, and
• higher advisory fees driven by higher industry-wide mergers and acquisitions ("M&A") activity and wallet share gains.

comparisons.peer_summary: Investment banking net revenues increased 35% to $6,170 million in 2024, driven by higher M&A advisory volumes, increased equity underwriting from IPOs and follow-ons, and higher fixed income underwriting from bond and loan issuances.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Morgan Stanley report strong double-digit growth in investment banking revenues for 2024, driven by recoveries in debt underwriting, equity underwriting, and advisory. Citi's Investment Banking revenues rose 38%, with DCM fees up 61% and equity fees up 38%. Morgan Stanley's net revenues for investment banking increased 35% to $6,170 million, driven by higher initial public offerings and follow-on offerings (equity), higher bond issuances (debt), and higher completed M&A transactions (advisory). The composition of growth is highly similar across both firms.
